nodes.label: Infinitive-to-Present Accent-Shift Rule (Verb Types)
nodes.rationale: An italicized infinitive in the verb-type appendix signals the word's accent falls on a different syllable in the present tense; the shift moves toward the beginning of the word for Types 1-2, 6-9, 11, 16, and toward the end of the word for Types 10 and 13-15 — applies even to unaccented-in-print words via a mentally-placed invisible accent mark.
nodes.community_name: Verbal Grammar: Aspect, Mood & Case Constructions
nodes.norm_label: infinitive-to-present accent-shift rule (verb types)

nodes.label: Verbal Aspect (Imperfective/Perfective) and Narrative Structure
nodes.rationale: Imperfective signals ongoing/habitual/general-standing-fact action; perfective usually denotes a single completed action but can also mark a repeated action when each instance's completion is emphasized. In narrative, perfective verbs advance plot while imperfective verbs set scene/background; the 'historic present' is a stylistic alternative for background narration.
nodes.community_name: Verbal Grammar: Aspect, Mood & Case Constructions
nodes.norm_label: verbal aspect (imperfective/perfective) and narrative structure

nodes.label: Whole-System B/C/S Dialect Showcase (Script + Jat Reflex + Lexicon Simultaneously)
nodes.rationale: Lesson 16's three letter-and-reply pairs are written as complete, self-consistent regional-standard specimens rather than isolated word-level [B]/[C]/[S] swaps: the Sarajevo pair is Ijekavian/Latin/Bosnian-lexicon; the Zagreb pair is Ijekavian/Latin/Croatian-lexicon with Croatian month names; the Belgrade pair is Ekavian and printed entirely in Cyrillic script with Serbian lexicon. This is the textbook's most sustained demonstration that script choice + jat reflex + lexicon co-vary as one bundled system rather than as independent word-for-word substitutions.
nodes.community_name: Verbal Grammar: Aspect, Mood & Case Constructions
nodes.norm_label: whole-system b/c/s dialect showcase (script + jat reflex + lexicon simultaneously)

nodes.label: B/C/S Bracket-Tagging Convention (Bosnian/Croatian/Serbian Standard-Variant Marking)
nodes.rationale: The textbook's core annotation convention: [B]/[C]/[S] (and combinations like [B,C], [B,S], [B,C,S]) mark which national standard(s) attest a given word, phrase, or grammatical form; applied consistently across vocabulary boxes, grammar exercises, and even Appendix 2's personal-name lists, where it further correlates with religious/cultural naming pools (Islamic/Ottoman-Turkic for [B], Catholic/Western-European for [C], Orthodox-Slavic for [S]).
nodes.community_name: Verbal Grammar: Aspect, Mood & Case Constructions
nodes.norm_label: b/c/s bracket-tagging convention (bosnian/croatian/serbian standard-variant marking)

nodes.label: BCS Collective Nouns (Singular Neuter/Feminine Group Nouns)
nodes.rationale: Collective nouns denote an object-group as an indivisible whole and are grammatically singular (mostly neuter: cveće/cvijeće, drveće, lišće, kàmenje; a second feminine-singular type for young creatures: ùnučad); regular individuated plurals exist but are comparatively rare.
nodes.community_name: Verbal Grammar: Aspect, Mood & Case Constructions
nodes.norm_label: bcs collective nouns (singular neuter/feminine group nouns)

nodes.label: BCS Conditional Mood (Formation and Uses)
nodes.rationale: Formed from L-participle + aorist-derived auxiliary (bih, bi, bi, bismo, biste, bi); used for politeness softening, toned-down statements/requests, three types of conditional sentences (ako+indicative / kad+conditional / da+present-conditional), and a purpose use with no direct English parallel.
nodes.community_name: Verbal Grammar: Aspect, Mood & Case Constructions
nodes.norm_label: bcs conditional mood (formation and uses)

nodes.label: Infinitive vs. da + Present Syntax Split (Croatian/Bosnian Infinitive-Favoring vs. Serbian da-Favoring)
nodes.rationale: A recurring modal-construction split attested repeatedly across this textbook's exercises: after a modal verb, Bosnian/Croatian favor the bare infinitive while Serbian substitutes da + present tense (e.g. treba odmah ìći vs. треба одмах да иде); Bosnian exercises show both strategies in use side by side.
nodes.community_name: Verbal Grammar: Aspect, Mood & Case Constructions
nodes.norm_label: infinitive vs. da + present syntax split (croatian/bosnian infinitive-favoring vs. serbian da-favoring)

nodes.label: Dative Logical-Subject / Experiencer Constructions (nedòstajati, pòći za rùkom, stalo je)
nodes.rationale: A family of BCS impersonal/experiencer verbs that invert English subject/object mapping: the thing experienced is the nominative grammatical subject (triggers agreement) while the person affected appears in an oblique (usually dative) case, e.g. nedòstajao mu je Zàgreb literally 'Zagreb was missing to him' = 'he missed Zagreb'.
nodes.community_name: Verbal Grammar: Aspect, Mood & Case Constructions
nodes.norm_label: dative logical-subject / experiencer constructions (nedostajati, poci za rukom, stalo je)

nodes.label: Indefinite-Forming Particles "god" and "bilo" (-ever)
nodes.rationale: Two alternative strategies for forming indefinite/universal pronouns and adverbs from question words: suffixing -god (kad god 'whenever', gdje god 'wherever') or prefixing bìlo (bìlo šta/što 'whatever', bìlo kòga 'whomever').
nodes.community_name: Verbal Grammar: Aspect, Mood & Case Constructions
nodes.norm_label: indefinite-forming particles "god" and "bilo" (-ever)

nodes.label: Croatian -irati vs. Bosnian/Serbian -ovati/-isati Loanword-Verb Formation Split
nodes.rationale: A recurring, productive pattern across this textbook's loanword verbs: Croatian standardly integrates a borrowed verb root with the -irati suffix, while Bosnian/Serbian use -ovati or -isati for the same root (e.g. interesìrati/interesovati, rezèrvirati/rezèrvisati, organizìrati/orgànizovati, angažìrati se/àngažovati se) — a systematic derivational-morphology difference, not merely a lexical swap.
nodes.community_name: Verbal Grammar: Aspect, Mood & Case Constructions
nodes.norm_label: croatian -irati vs. bosnian/serbian -ovati/-isati loanword-verb formation split

nodes.label: Montenegrin as a Distinct Ijekavian BCS Variant
nodes.rationale: The textbook identifies Montenegrin as a fourth national standard (advising students to follow [J]/[S] forms since it gets no bracket-letter of its own) marked by: systematic ijekavian character extending into negated biti (nijèsam/nijèsi) and archaic-elsewhere adjectival endings (starijem); consonant realization of tj/dj as ć/đ (tjerati→ćerati, djèvojka→đèvojka, gdje→đe); and characteristic vocabulary (sjutra, zbòriti). Montenegrin vocabulary is noted to have more in common with Serbian than Bosnian or Croatian.
nodes.community_name: Verbal Grammar: Aspect, Mood & Case Constructions
nodes.norm_label: montenegrin as a distinct ijekavian bcs variant

nodes.label: Passive and Impersonal Sentence Formation (se-verb vs. biti + participle)
nodes.rationale: Two passive strategies: a se-verb (agrees in number with subject, foregrounds the action) or biti + passive participle (agrees in gender/number, foregrounds the result); most verbs favor one strategy, roditi se is a rare verb allowing both; impersonal sentences are always 3sg with a neuter-singular participle.
nodes.community_name: Verbal Grammar: Aspect, Mood & Case Constructions
nodes.norm_label: passive and impersonal sentence formation (se-verb vs. biti + participle)

nodes.label: Reciprocal "Each Other" (jèdan ... drugi, Gender Agreement)
nodes.rationale: BCS expresses 'each other' either via a reflexive se-verb or via jèdan drugi (two participants) / jèdni drugi (larger group); the second element takes whatever case the governing verb/preposition requires.
nodes.community_name: Verbal Grammar: Aspect, Mood & Case Constructions
nodes.norm_label: reciprocal "each other" (jedan ... drugi, gender agreement)

nodes.label: Relative Conjunction Kòji (Gender/Number vs. Case Agreement)
nodes.rationale: Kòji's gender/number is fixed by its antecedent, but its case is fixed independently by its own clause role; BCS can never omit it where English can omit 'that/which'.
nodes.community_name: Verbal Grammar: Aspect, Mood & Case Constructions
nodes.norm_label: relative conjunction koji (gender/number vs. case agreement)

nodes.label: BCS 16-Type Verb Conjugation System
nodes.rationale: The textbook's organizing framework (introduced Lesson 10, elaborated through the book) sorting every BCS verb into 16 numbered present-tense-stem-formation types plus two named mixed subtypes (Type 5(inf.)/7(pres.), Type 12(inf.)/14(pres.)) and an irregular class (biti, hteti/htjeti) outside the system; each type is defined by an infinitive+1sg-present model-verb pair.
nodes.community_name: Verbal Grammar: Aspect, Mood & Case Constructions
nodes.norm_label: bcs 16-type verb conjugation system

nodes.label: Present and Past Verbal Adverbs (-ći / -vši Converbs)
nodes.rationale: Present verbal adverb (-ći, from 3pl present of imperfectives) marks simultaneous action; past verbal adverb (-vši, from perfective L-participle) marks prior completed action; both are literary-register converbs, a few of which (ìdući, bivši) have become full adjectives.

nodes.label: Sarajevo/Zagreb Syllable-Switching Slang — a genuine, historically attested colloquial word-game mechanism in Bosnian/Croatian speech, structurally comparable to English pig-Latin-style play, in which a word's syllables are switched to produce a new slang form. Two attested historical layers: (1) a Sarajevo colloquial layer (vozdra < zdravo 'hi', zemka < kazem 'I say', dido < dodji 'come!', zibje < bjezi 'run!'); (2) an older Zagreb layer, most widespread in the 1960s, of which a handful of terms remain in occasional use today (lima < mali 'kid', cobra < braco 'bro', Somi < the name 'Miso', Njofra < the name 'Franjo' — this last surviving longer than the rest specifically because a Croatian cartoon dub popularized it as a catchphrase form of address). The source explicitly contrasts this with Belgrade's own extensive slang system, which does NOT use syllable-switching — making it a geographically-bounded (Sarajevo/Zagreb, not Belgrade) mechanism rather than a pan-BCS slang strategy. This is a productive, rule-governed word-formation process distinct from ordinary lexical borrowing or dialectal variation, and is the strongest direct evidence in this corpus of an actual slang-generating MECHANISM (as opposed to a slang vocabulary item) — directly relevant to this project's goal of deriving conlang slang mechanics from real-language precedent.
nodes.rationale: Selected as this language's flagship mechanism because it is a genuine generative slang-formation RULE (transferable to a conlang's phonology) rather than a single borrowed word or register marker; its geographic boundedness (attested Sarajevo/older Zagreb, explicitly NOT Belgrade) also gives it real sociolinguistic texture rather than being a vague pan-regional claim.
